title: Supernova 2026ahvu peaks this week beside star clusters under 100 million years old
excerpt: The Type Ia supernova in the galaxy NGC 1433 keeps brightening toward a peak between 18 and 23 November. Archival Hubble and Webb images place it between two st
content:
A white dwarf in a nearby spiral galaxy has blown itself apart, and its light is still climbing. In the first few days after astronomers spotted it, the explosion grew more than twentyfold brighter, and it should keep rising until a modest backyard telescope can pick it out.

The brightness is only half the story. Hubble and Webb images taken years before the blast show the spot where it went off sitting between two young star clusters. If the exploding star belongs to either one, the system that produced it formed less than a hundred million years ago, while most exploding white dwarfs take billions of years to detonate.

The supernova, catalogued as SN 2026ahvu, lies in NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy in the southern constellation Horologium. The asteroid-hunting ATLAS survey caught it as a faint point of light at magnitude 17, and a Keck II spectrum the next day identified a young Type Ia supernova: the thermonuclear destruction of a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a star like the Sun.

NSF NOIRLab, which released new images of the explosion from the Gemini South telescope and the Dark Energy Camera in Chile, expects the peak within the coming week or so, at a brightness that small amateur telescopes can reach from southern skies.

Why a young neighbourhood matters

Type Ia supernovae are the standard candles of cosmology. They all reach roughly the same peak brightness, so how bright one looks from Earth reveals its distance, and these explosions showed that the expansion of the universe is speeding up. They also forge much of the iron in the cosmos. Yet astronomers still debate which kind of star system produces them.

A white dwarf cannot explode on its own. It needs a partner, either an ordinary star feeding it gas or a second white dwarf that merges with it, and the waiting time between a system’s birth and its explosion, called the delay time, hints at which route is at work. Surveys of whole galaxies suggest two populations: a delayed group that waits billions of years, and a prompt group that explodes within a few hundred million years. The prompt group has only ever been detected statistically, through averages over many galaxies, never pinned to one explosion with a known age.

There is a floor on how prompt an explosion can be. Only stars below about eight times the Sun’s mass end as white dwarfs, and the heaviest of those live roughly 40 million years. A supernova next to a 37-million-year-old cluster would sit almost on that floor. The authors of a new preprint put it plainly: if the explosion belongs to the younger cluster, “it would imply that Type Ia SNe can occur almost immediately after white dwarf formation.”

How they did it

The team, led by Sumit Sarbadhicary of Johns Hopkins University, needed no new observations. The PHANGS survey had already mapped NGC 1433 with Hubble, from ultraviolet to near-infrared light, and with Webb’s infrared camera. The group placed the supernova’s position, known to about a tenth of an arcsecond, on those archival frames.

Two compact clusters appeared right beside it, one 0.19 arcseconds to the north and the other 0.26 arcseconds to the south. Depending on which distance to the galaxy is correct, that puts them between roughly 26 and 80 light-years from the explosion site. The automated PHANGS catalogue had listed only the northern one.

To date the clusters, the researchers measured their light in ten filters and fitted the colours with models of ageing star populations. Neither shows the glowing hydrogen or warm dust around newborn stars, so both are older than about ten million years. Both still shine in ultraviolet light, which fades once the hottest stars die, so neither is more than a few hundred million years old. The fits give about 37 million years for the northern cluster and about 95 million years for the southern one. Using Hubble data alone, without Webb, the estimates shift to 57 and 88 million years.

A galaxy with two distances

No one agrees how far away NGC 1433 is. One measurement, based on the brightest red giant stars, gives about 30 million light-years, though its authors flagged it as uncertain. Another, based on the glow of planetary nebulae, gives about 62 million light-years. NOIRLab’s release adopts roughly 50 million.

The supernova itself should settle the argument. A typical Type Ia peaks at an absolute magnitude near minus 19.3, a fixed brightness that astronomers then compare with what they see from Earth. At the nearer distance it would appear at roughly magnitude 10.5. At the farther one it would appear at roughly 12.1, and that is the spread in NOIRLab’s forecast. “The imminent peak of the SN Ia light curve will provide a swift resolution to any distance controversy,” the preprint’s authors write.

The cluster ages do not depend on the distance, though their masses do: a few thousand Suns for the northern cluster and up to about 11,000 for the southern one. For comparison, NOIRLab ranks the explosion among the nearest Type Ia supernovae seen since SN 2011fe in the Pinwheel Galaxy, about 21 million light-years away. SN 2014J, in the galaxy M82, was closer still, at about 11 million light-years. Neither of those has been tied to a young star cluster.

What it doesn’t settle

The study is a preprint submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters and has not yet been peer reviewed. Its claim rests on proximity on the sky, which is not proof of a physical link. The team estimates that only about 0.4 percent of the galaxy’s starlight lies as close to a catalogued cluster as the supernova does, so a chance alignment with an older star is unlikely. If any patch of ultraviolet light is counted instead of confirmed clusters, the chance rises to about 4 percent.

Which cluster is the birthplace is also open. The supernova sits slightly closer to the northern cluster, but the difference is about the size of the positional error. The northern cluster is light, and the explosion lies at about five times its visible radius, so the authors favour the heavier southern cluster, from which a system moving at about five kilometres per second could have drifted to the explosion site in a few million years. In small clusters, random variation in how many massive stars form can also skew age estimates.

Albert Kong of National Tsing Hua University checked archival Chandra X-ray Observatory images, about 95,000 seconds in total, and found no X-ray source at the position, which rules out only the most luminous X-ray sources that some progenitor models predict. A team led by Yvette Cendes of the University of Oregon observed the site with the MeerKAT radio telescope about five days after discovery and detected no radio signal, which so far shows no sign of the dense gas that some progenitor scenarios leave around the star. None of this yet tells the partner-star and white-dwarf-merger scenarios apart.

When and where to look

ATLAS discovered the explosion on 2 November 2026. The GOTO survey later found a faint trace of it in images from 1 November and nothing on 30 October, so the explosion was caught within a few days of first light. Keck classified it on 3 November, amateur observers reported it near magnitude 12.3 by 10 November, and NOIRLab released its images on 12 November.

NOIRLab expects the supernova to peak between magnitude 10.5 and 12.1 between 18 and 23 November, a forecast that may shift as data come in. That is far too faint for the naked eye but within reach of telescopes of about 10 to 15 centimetres in aperture or larger under dark skies, and cameras can record it with less. The galaxy sits about 47 degrees south of the celestial equator, so observers in South America, southern Africa and Australia have the best view. From latitudes like those of Madrid, New York or Beijing it barely clears the horizon, if at all.

Common questions about SN 2026ahvu

What is a Type Ia supernova?

It is the explosion of a white dwarf, the compact remnant of a Sun-like star, after it gains mass from a companion or merges with another white dwarf. Because these blasts peak at a predictable brightness, astronomers use them to measure cosmic distances.

Can I see SN 2026ahvu with a telescope?

Yes, from southern latitudes, with an amateur telescope under dark skies. It should peak between 18 and 23 November in NGC 1433, in the constellation Horologium, and stays very low or below the horizon from Europe and most of North America.

How far away is SN 2026ahvu?

Its host galaxy, NGC 1433, is somewhere between about 30 and 62 million light-years away, depending on which published distance is right. NOIRLab uses about 50 million light-years. The supernova’s peak brightness should narrow that range.

What is a prompt Type Ia supernova?

It is a white dwarf explosion that happens within a few hundred million years of its stars forming, rather than billions of years later. Prompt events were known only from statistics; SN 2026ahvu may be the first tied to star clusters of measured age.

Over the next few weeks, Gemini, the Dark Energy Camera and the SOAR telescope in Chile will track the explosion’s colour, brightness and spectrum through the peak and into the fade. The preprint has been submitted for peer review. When the peak arrives, the supernova will measure the distance to its own galaxy, and astronomers will then know how far it sits from the clusters that may have produced it.

Reference: Sarbadhicary et al., “SN 2026ahvu in NGC 1433 May Be a Prompt Type Ia Supernova with a Delay Time Under 100 Myr,” arXiv preprint submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2026. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2611.09875
